questions.prompt: A lorry unloading sacks of seed and fertiliser at a village farming co-operative carries three letters on its side and nothing else: FAO. Four international bodies stand on the district officer's list. Which of them has been folded into those three letters?

options.text: World Food Programme
World Trade Organization
Food and Agriculture Organization
United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund

questions.explanation: Unfold the letters one at a time and each has to hand you a word, in the order they are printed: F for food, A for agriculture, O for the organization that joins them. The body that feeds hungry people is a tempting answer beside a lorry full of seed, but its own initials spell out three different words and none of them opens on an F - seed and fertiliser go to a farm, not to a canteen. The body that deals in trade has been folded down to three quite different letters, and the long name of the children's fund needs six.

questions.prompt: A report on a mountain district reads: "The bridge was carried away in November and the road stayed cut until March. Forty of the youngest children therefore spent that winter at home." What work is the word therefore doing between those two sentences?

options.text: it presents the second sentence as the result of the first one
it presents the second sentence as an objection to the first
it presents the second sentence as one example among several
it presents the second sentence as a condition set on the first

questions.explanation: This little word joins a cause to what came out of it: the water took the bridge, so the smallest children could not reach the school. Take it out and you are left with two facts standing side by side; put it back and you have claimed that the second happened because of the first. Nothing here contradicts anything, which is the job of a word like however; nothing is being illustrated, which is what for example would announce; and no condition is being set, since both events have already happened and neither depends on the other coming true.

questions.prompt: In 2001/02, across the world, 115 million children of primary age were out of school. One single region held 24.0 million of them - roughly one out of every five in the whole count. Which region was it?

options.text: South Asia
Eastern and Southern Africa
East Asia and the Pacific
West and Central Africa

questions.explanation: Twenty-four million out of a hundred and fifteen is a fifth of the total, or 20.8 per cent, and one region carried that: the western and central belt of Africa. It is not the heaviest slice of the circle - South Asia is far heavier, with 42.3 million children and more than a third of the world's total, so a region holding one fifth cannot be that one. Below it the figures fall away quickly: the eastern and southern belt of Africa held 21.4 million, and the Pacific side of Asia only 10.0 million, which is well under half of what the question describes.

questions.prompt: A caretaker pins a notice on the door of the gymnasium: "If the heating is not repaired, the hall will not be used in January." Which sentence puts exactly the same warning into a sentence with unless?

options.text: Unless the heating is not repaired, the hall will not be used in January.
Unless the heating is repaired, the hall will not be used in January.
Unless the heating is repaired, the hall will be used in January.
Unless the heating is not repaired, the hall will be used in January.

questions.explanation: One word does the work of two here. Since unless already carries the sense of if not, the verb standing behind it has to be left positive; write a second not there and you have said the reverse of the notice, promising a closed hall to whoever mends the heating. And the far half of the sentence was never in question: the caretaker's warning is about a hall that stays shut, so that half keeps its own negative untouched, whichever of the two openings you choose. Change both halves at once, as two of these sentences do, and the notice ends up announcing exactly what the caretaker feared it would not.

questions.prompt: In the middle of a charity's full page, in letters larger than anything else printed on it, stands a single line: "Grade 2 + $1 = Grade 3". Read as a sentence, what is that line promising the reader?

options.text: that a place in the third year of school is sold for one dollar a year
that a child in the second year must find a dollar himself to move up
that one dollar can carry a child from one school year into the next
that the charity has already collected one dollar from each of its readers

questions.explanation: Read the sum from left to right and it says: a child who has reached one year, plus a very small amount of money, comes out at the year above. The gift is what bridges the two, and the whole point of writing it as arithmetic is to make that bridge look short and certain. Notice who is meant to pay: the reader holding the page, not the child, who is the one thing in the sum that is not being asked for anything. Nor is a place being sold - the sum names a gift, not a price - and nothing in it looks backwards at money already gathered; a page that had finished collecting would have no reason to be printed at all.
